title: Concentration and Scalability
intro: Why adding qubits does not automatically add usable features: expectation values concentrate exponentially under scrambling and noise, every feature must be estimated from shots, measurement forces restarts, and classical simulation has its own scaling.

blocks.text: The promise and the catch

The case for quantum reservoirs starts from dimension: $n$ qubits carry a state with $4^n - 1$ real parameters, so the reservoir could in principle offer exponentially many features. The catch is that a feature is an expectation value $\operatorname{Tr}(O\rho_k)$, and what the readout sees is its estimate from $S$ single-shot measurements, with standard error about $\sqrt{(1 - \langle O\rangle^2)/S}$ for a Pauli $O$. A feature is useful only if it moves with the input by more than that error. Concentration is the statement that, for generic dynamics, it does not.
Exponential concentration under scrambling

Suppose the reservoir dynamics are scrambling enough that, as the input varies, the state $\vert\psi\rangle$ behaves like a Haar-random state on $D = 2^n$ dimensions (it suffices that the induced ensemble of unitaries is a unitary 2-design). For a Pauli string $P \ne I$, $\operatorname{Tr}P = 0$ and $P^2 = I$, and the Haar second moment gives

blocks.caption: Variance of a Pauli expectation over Haar-random states: $1/(2^n + 1)$.

blocks.text: So the spread of every Pauli feature across inputs falls as $1/\sqrt{2^n+1}$: 0.24 at 4 qubits, 0.031 at 10, $3\times10^{-5}$ at 30. Chebyshev then says that for all but a fraction $\delta$ of inputs the feature sits within $1/\sqrt{\delta(2^n+1)}$ of its mean: the features of different inputs become exponentially hard to tell apart. Xiong and co-authors analyse this for quantum extreme learning machines (memoryless reservoirs), identifying randomness, hardware noise, entanglement and global measurements as sources of concentration, alongside a Fourier-spectrum view of what the encoding can express; Thanasilp and co-authors give the matching result for quantum kernels, and the same mechanism underlies barren plateaus in trained circuits (McClean and co-authors).
Resolving a change of a fraction $\varepsilon$ of that spread needs a standard error below $\varepsilon/\sqrt{D+1}$, so

blocks.caption: Shots per feature per time step to resolve input dependence under full scrambling.

widget.title: Concentration: the spread of a feature and the shots to read it

blocks.text: The two curves are mirror images: every halving of the spread quadruples the shots. At $\varepsilon = 0.1$, 10 qubits need about $10^5$ shots per feature per step and 30 qubits about $10^{11}$. Set $\varepsilon$ to 0.5 and the shot line drops by $\log_{10} 25 \approx 1.4$ but keeps the same slope: no constant-factor trick escapes $2^n$.

Concentration is about generic, fully scrambled dynamics. Reservoirs that work stay away from it: they read local, low-weight observables after short evolution, so the light cone limits scrambling; they use disorder or symmetries that keep the dynamics from exploring the whole space; and the reset injection keeps refreshing a qubit with a state that depends strongly on the input. The Dynamical Regimes (#/qrc/models/dynamical-regimes) page shows that performance peaks at intermediate fields, not in the most chaotic regime.
Concentration from noise

Noise produces the same symptom by another road. Under a global depolarizing channel of strength $p$ per step, $\rho \mapsto (1-p)\rho + p\,I/D$, every traceless feature shrinks by $(1-p)$ each step. Local noise on deep circuits behaves similarly: with depolarizing probability $p$ per gate on a weight-$w$ observable the signal falls roughly like $(1-p)^{\#\text{gates in its light cone}}$. A reservoir needs some dissipation to forget (the echo state property), so the design question is a window: enough contraction to fade old inputs within the memory you need, not so much that the input-dependent part of every feature drowns. Sannia and co-authors and Kubota and co-authors study this window; see Dissipation as a Resource (#/qrc/models/dissipation-as-resource).

blocks.caption: Both come from contraction; they differ in what contracts and how fast.

blocks.text: The effective number of features

Put the two effects into one quantity. Let $\Sigma$ be the covariance of the exact features over the input distribution, with eigenvalues $\sigma_1^2 \ge \sigma_2^2 \ge \dots$, and let shot noise add roughly independent variance $1/S$ per feature. A ridge readout can use a direction only if its signal variance beats the noise, so a useful proxy is

blocks.caption: Effective number of features: each direction counts fully if its signal variance exceeds the noise variance $1/S$, and hardly at all if not.

blocks.text: Adding qubits raises the number of directions but, under concentration, lowers each $\sigma_i^2$; past some size $N_{\text{eff}}$ stops growing at fixed $S$. The hands-on sample shows the onset on a small system: a 4-qubit, 20-feature reservoir has memory capacity 3.86 exact, 3.53 at $10^4$ shots, 2.80 at $10^3$ and 1.94 at $10^2$.
The cost of measurement in time

A projective measurement of the reservoir destroys the state the next steps need. The simplest faithful protocol therefore restarts: to get the features at step $k$, prepare the initial state, feed inputs $1..k$, measure, and repeat $S$ times. Over a series of length $T$ that costs

blocks.caption: Restart protocol: quadratic in the series length.

blocks.text: Fading memory rescues most of it: only the last $L$ inputs matter (to precision $\lambda^L$), so each feature can be computed from a run that starts $L$ steps back, costing $S\,T\,L$. Online protocols go further, using weak measurements, partial measurements or rewinding to keep the run going; see Measurement Back-Action (#/qrc/hardware/measurement-back-action) and Online Protocols (#/qrc/hardware/online-protocols) (Mujal and co-authors; Yasuda and co-authors).
Classical simulation cost
The other side of scalability is what a classical computer pays to reproduce the reservoir, which sets the bar any advantage claim has to clear.

items: Exact density matrix: $4^n$ complex numbers, 16 bytes each, so $16 \cdot 4^n$ bytes: 4 GiB at $n = 14$, 16 GiB at $n = 15$, and each step costs $O(8^n)$ with dense matrices.

Quantum trajectories: the reset is a measure-and-prepare channel, so averaging over random measurement outcomes of qubit 1 reproduces $\rho_k$ exactly. A state-vector simulation of one trajectory needs $16 \cdot 2^n$ bytes (16 GiB at $n = 30$), and $M$ trajectories give each feature to precision about $1/\sqrt{M}$, the same scaling as $S$ hardware shots. The classical simulation inherits the same shot-noise problem the device has, but not more.

Structured dynamics: a one-dimensional nearest-neighbour transverse-field Ising chain maps to free fermions, so its unitary part is simulable in polynomial time; Gaussian continuous-variable reservoirs are simulable through their covariance matrices; low-entanglement dynamics yield to tensor networks. A reservoir in one of these classes can still be a good reservoir, but not a quantum advantage.

blocks.text: Worked problems

blocks.title: Shots for ten scrambled qubits
blocks.text: A fully scrambling 10-qubit reservoir is read through Pauli features. How many shots per feature per time step are needed to resolve input-driven changes of 10% of a feature's spread?
solution: We need standard error $1/\sqrt{S}$ below $0.1 \times 0.031$, so $S \ge 1025/0.01$.

blocks.title: Restart versus windowed restart
blocks.text: A time series of $T = 1000$ steps is processed with $S = 1000$ shots per step. How many reservoir steps are executed with full restarts, and with restarts from a window of $L = 20$ steps?
solution: The window is justified if the reservoir's contraction factor $\lambda$ satisfies $\lambda^{20}$ well below the shot error; for the 4-qubit reservoir of the hands-on sample, which contracts by about 0.82 per step, $0.82^{20} \approx 0.019$, comparable to the shot error at $S = 1000$ (about 0.03).

blocks.title: Memory for an exact simulation
blocks.text: How many qubits can an exact density-matrix simulation hold in 64 GiB, storing one complex128 matrix?
solution: Memory is $16 \cdot 4^n$ bytes, and 64 GiB is $2^{36}$ bytes.
In practice the propagator and a work copy need two or three more matrices of the same size, so 15 qubits is the realistic limit.
